missions.title: A new home for the pandas
missions.intro: Three texts about the same thing: a new Panda House at a wildlife park.

texts.title: Panda House opening day

body.p: Marlow Wildlife Park is proud to open its new Panda House on Saturday 14 June. Come and meet Lan and Bo, our two giant pandas.
On the day you can:

ul: watch the pandas eat their breakfast at 10:00
ask a keeper your questions at 11:30
have your face painted in the Bamboo Café
pick up a free panda trail map at the gate

body.p: Entry is free for everyone on opening day. Please arrive early, because the Panda House can only hold 200 people at a time.

texts.title: Behind the scenes at the Panda House

body.p: It took 14 months to build the new Panda House at Marlow Wildlife Park, and almost every detail was planned with the pandas in mind. Head keeper Priya Nair showed us around before the doors opened to the public.

body.h: A home that feels like a forest

body.p: Each panda has its own indoor room, which is kept cool all year, and a large outdoor garden. Giant pandas come from the mountain forests of south-west China, so the garden has hills to climb, trees for shade and a small stream. "Pandas are happiest when there is plenty to climb and somewhere shady to rest," says Priya.

Bamboo makes up almost all of a giant panda's diet, but it gives very little energy, so pandas spend much of the day eating. The park grows some of its own bamboo. The rest arrives fresh by lorry every week from a specialist grower (you can see the grower's farm on the map on page 4). Keepers check every delivery by hand and throw away any stalks that look dry.

Keepers start at 7:00 am by checking that both pandas are well. Next they clean the rooms and prepare the first feed. A team of six keepers will look after Lan and Bo, and a vet visits every month to check that they are healthy. They also hide small treats around the garden so that the pandas have to search for them. This is called enrichment, and it stops the pandas from getting bored.
Visitors may find the pandas asleep. "Please don't be disappointed," Priya adds. "A sleeping panda is a healthy, relaxed panda."
The Panda House is, without doubt, the best thing to happen to Marlow in years. Entry is free on opening day, but the park expects it to be very busy.

texts.title: Our first visit to the Panda House

body.p: We went on opening day with my sister's kids, who are six and nine, and to be honest I'm still recovering! It was the busiest day I have seen at Marlow for ages.

The Panda House is gorgeous. The garden looks just like a real forest, and Bo was brilliant. He sat on a rock eating bamboo for ages. The kids loved watching him. The keeper talk at 11:30 was great as well. She told us that Lan and Bo spend most of the day eating, and my nine-year-old asked three questions in a row!
We queued for nearly an hour, and by the time we got inside Lan was fast asleep in the corner. The Bamboo Café was packed, and I paid £4 for a tiny cup of tea. I was gutted!

ul: Get there early, before the gates open if you can.
Bring a packed lunch, because the café queue is huge.
Check the feeding times on the website first, so you don't miss Bo at breakfast.
Wear comfy shoes. You will walk loads.

body.p: Would I go again? Definitely, but on a quiet weekday!

missions.title: Helping the pandas
missions.intro: Three texts about adopting a panda and how pandas are protected.

texts.title: Adopt a panda

body.p: Help to look after the giant pandas at Ferndale Zoo by becoming a panda adopter. Ferndale Zoo is home to two giant pandas, who arrived last year. They love to eat, play and sleep in the sun.

body.box: **Your adoption pack:** a certificate, a photo of your panda, a cuddly toy and a free family ticket.

body.p: Adopting costs just £4 a month. Your money pays for the pandas' bamboo, health checks and toys. You can sign up at the zoo shop or online, and it only takes five minutes.

texts.title: How are giant pandas helped in the wild?

body.p: Giant pandas live in only a few mountain areas of China, and they depend on bamboo forests for food and shelter. Years ago, many of these forests were cleared to make room for farms and new buildings. As the forests shrank, the pandas lost their homes.

To help the pandas, China has set up protected nature reserves, where trees cannot be cut down. There are now dozens of reserves across the mountains, and together they protect large areas of forest. Rangers walk through the forests every week to check on the wildlife. They look for paw prints and droppings, and they also place cameras that take photographs when an animal walks past.

Many pandas now live in small patches of forest that are cut off from each other. The corridors – strips of forest that join one area to another – allow pandas to move safely between patches, so that they can find food and meet mates. Planting new bamboo along the corridors takes years, but the forest is slowly joining up again. "Without the corridors, the pandas would be trapped," says ranger Li Na.

Zoos cannot return pandas to the wild by themselves, but they can still make a difference. Money raised by zoos and their visitors helps to pay for the reserves and the rangers. Zoos also run breeding programmes, so that scientists can learn how to care for baby pandas. Visitors can also help by adopting a panda, which pays for food and care.

Conservation work takes many years, and it is not easy. Even so, the work to save the giant panda is the most inspiring conservation story of recent times. Nothing is more important than protecting the forests where these animals live.

texts.title: Our class adopted a panda. Will you?

body.p: Last term, Year 10 voted to adopt a giant panda. Why? In geography we learned that pandas are losing their forest homes, and we wanted to do something about it.

Imagine a world without pandas. Some people ask why we should care about animals so far away. We believe that every living thing matters, and pandas are a symbol of hope for nature all over the world. Would you want a world without them? Of course not! Every pound we raise helps to pay for bamboo, health checks and toys, so it really does make a difference.

We have already raised £86 from our cake sale, but we need your help to reach £200 by the end of term. Our teacher, Mr Dale, thinks we can do it, and we are determined to prove him right. It will be fun, and you will be helping a great cause.
Here is how you can help:

ul: Donate any amount at the school office.
Join our sponsored silent hour on Friday.
Bake something for our second cake sale.

body.p: Just £2 buys a day's bamboo for one panda, so please give whatever you can. Together, we can help to protect these amazing animals!

missions.title: Floating in the Dead Sea
missions.intro: Three texts about a day at the Dead Sea in Israel.

texts.title: Dead Sea day trip

body.p: Float in the famous Dead Sea on a relaxed day out from Tel Aviv. Our friendly guide will tell you all about the area on the journey.
A minibus, towels, a picnic lunch and entry to the beach.
We leave at 8:00 am and return at 5:00 pm. Please be at the meeting point ten minutes early.
Sun cream, a hat and sandals that you can wear in the water.
Adults £45. Children under 14 £30.

texts.title: Floating in the Dead Sea: what to expect

body.p: The Dead Sea is one of the most unusual places in the world. It sits more than 400 metres below sea level, which makes it the lowest place on land on Earth, and its water is so salty that it holds your body up. Even people who cannot swim can lie back and float.

body.h: How to get the most from your visit

body.p: Local guide Noa Levi has taken hundreds of visitors to the Dead Sea, and she has some simple advice. "Walk in slowly, sit down in the water and then lean back," she says. "Never put your head under, and keep splashing to a minimum. Salt water in the eyes really stings."

Salt water also stings tiny cuts, so avoid shaving on the morning of your visit. Most people stay in the water for a short time (about 15 minutes is enough), because the salt can dry out your skin. Afterwards, rinse off in the fresh water showers on the beach, which also has changing rooms nearby.

Many visitors cover themselves in the dark mud from the shore. The mud is full of minerals, and it makes your skin feel wonderfully soft. Let it dry for a few minutes in the sun, then wash it off in the sea. Do not forget to take a camera, but keep it somewhere dry!

It can be extremely hot by the Dead Sea, even in the early morning. Wear a hat, put on plenty of sun cream and drink lots of fresh water. Wear sandals, too, because the stones on the shore can be sharp. Children should always stay close to an adult in the water.
Floating there is the most relaxing thing you can do on holiday, and it is an experience you will never forget.

texts.source: Travel Talk forum, thread: "Is the Dead Sea day trip worth it?"
texts.title: Re: Is the Dead Sea day trip worth it?

body.p: Hi! I went last spring with two friends and I'd say yes, it's worth it, but go early. The guide on our minibus was lovely and told us loads about the desert on the way, which made the long journey go quickly.

Floating was the weirdest and funniest thing I've ever done. You just lie back and the water holds you up, no effort at all! We took loads of photos of each other reading the paper, which I know everyone does.

The not-so-great bits: the beach was packed by 11 o'clock and it was boiling. I splashed water in my eye and it stung like mad, so listen when they tell you not to put your head under. The salt also dries on your skin and feels sticky, so use the showers. The picnic lunch was a bit boring too: just a cheese sandwich and an apple. Overall though, I'd go again in a heartbeat.
My tips:

ul: Go as early as you can.
Take a bottle of fresh water to drink and to rinse your face.
Wear sandals, because the stones are sharp.
Don't forget sun cream.

body.p: Hope that helps. Has anyone else been?

missions.title: Markets and food
missions.intro: Three texts about food in Israel.

texts.title: Easy shakshuka

body.p: Shakshuka is a tasty breakfast dish from Israel. It is made with eggs cooked in a spicy tomato sauce.
You will need: **4 eggs**, **1 onion**, **2 red peppers**, **1 tin of tomatoes** and **1 teaspoon of cumin**.

Cook the chopped onion and peppers for ten minutes. Add the tomatoes and cumin, then cook for five more minutes. Next, crack the eggs into the sauce and cook until they are firm. Serve with fresh bread. It takes about thirty minutes to make, and it serves four people.

texts.title: Eating your way around the markets of Israel

body.p: If you want to understand a country, visit its food markets. In Israel, the biggest markets, such as the Carmel Market in Tel Aviv and the Mahane Yehuda Market in Jerusalem, are noisy, colourful places where stallholders shout out their prices and the smell of fresh bread fills the air. Markets are also where local people do their everyday shopping, not just tourists. Allow at least two hours to explore.

Almost every market has a stall selling falafel, which are crispy balls made from chickpeas, usually served in warm pitta bread with salad. You will also find hummus, a smooth dip made from chickpeas, tahini (a paste made from sesame seeds) and lemon. Many cafés serve small dishes called "mezze", which are shared by everyone at the table. Fresh pitta is baked in the market every hour, so it is often still warm when you buy it.

Look out for the spice stalls, which sell bags of colourful spices piled high in sacks. There are also stalls selling fresh fruit and vegetables, olives, cheese, dried fruit and nuts. Many vendors are happy to let customers taste before they buy. Some markets also have musicians, so you can enjoy a tune while you shop.

Friday is the busiest day. Many shops close for Shabbat, the day of rest, which begins on Friday evening, so people shop for the weekend before it starts. Food writer Yael Cohen advises going in the morning: "The crowds are smaller and the fruit and vegetables are at their freshest."
Whatever time you go, bring cash and wear comfortable shoes. The falafel at the Carmel Market is the best in the world, and you will fall in love with the food.

texts.title: Review: Tel Aviv market food tour

body.p: Rating: 4 out of 5 stars
We booked this three-hour food tour on our second day in Tel Aviv, and it was a delicious way to see the city. Our guide, Dani, was friendly and funny, and he knew everyone at the market.

The best part was the tasting stops. We tried warm falafel, creamy hummus and sweet, sticky pastries, and every single dish was fantastic. Dani also took us to a spice stall, where we learned how to tell fresh spices from old ones. He also told us the story behind each dish, and he gave us a map so we could find our favourite stalls again the next day. The tour started on time and finished exactly when promised.
However, the tour was too crowded. There were 25 people in our group, so it was hard to hear Dani over the noise of the market. It was also very hot, and we only stopped for water once.
Top tips:

ul: Come hungry, because there is a lot to eat.
Wear a hat and bring a bottle of water.
Book the morning tour to avoid the crowds.

body.p: I would definitely recommend this tour, but only if the group were smaller!

missions.title: Park and Ride
missions.intro: Three texts about travelling by train and by bus.

texts.title: Fennline Trains

body.p: Home | Tickets | Timetables | Railcards | Contact us
Welcome to Fennline Trains. We run fast, friendly services between Fennbridge, Kettlewick and Ashby Cross every day of the week. Tickets can be bought online, at the station or on board.
Travelling with a bike? Bikes travel free on all our trains, except between 7:00 am and 9:30 am on weekdays, when the trains are at their busiest.
Need some help with your journey? Please speak to a member of staff at any station. They will be glad to help.

texts.title: Park and Ride: is it worth it?

body.p: Kettlewick's new Park and Ride opened in March, and thousands of drivers have already tried it. Local people have given it a warm welcome. The idea is simple. Drivers leave their cars at the edge of town and take a bus into the centre, which takes about ten minutes.

The car park has 600 spaces and parking costs £3 for the whole day. A bus leaves every eight minutes from 6:30 am until 7:00 pm. Parking also covers your bus fare, so there is nothing more to pay. The car park is lit at night so that drivers feel safe, and staff are on duty all day to help.

Commuters and shoppers are the biggest users, and shoppers like it too. "I used to spend half an hour driving round looking for a space," says Imran Shah, who works in a bank in the town centre. "Now I park, read my book on the bus, and I'm at my desk before nine."

Parking in the town centre can cost up to £9 for a day, so the Park and Ride is much cheaper. Regular users can save even more with a season ticket (a ticket that lets you travel as often as you like for a month or a year). The council says the scheme will pay for itself within five years.

Not quite. Some passengers complain that the buses are full during the morning peak, when many people are travelling to work or school. A council spokesperson said that extra buses will be added if they are needed.
Even so, it is the best idea the council has had for years. If you drive into town every day, you should try it.

texts.title: Subject: Park and Ride report!

body.p: Hi Jess,

Guess what? I tried the new Park and Ride in Kettlewick on Saturday and it was loads better than I expected. Parking was only £3, which is a bargain compared with the £9 I paid in town last month. The bus turned up after about two minutes and the driver was really friendly.

The downside? We went at 8:15 and the bus was rammed, so I had to stand all the way into town (it only took ten minutes, thankfully). The ride itself was lovely. There was Wi-Fi on the bus, so I caught up on my messages, and the seats were really comfy. Also, the last bus back is at 7:00 pm, which is far too early if you fancy a night out!
My tips if you go:

ul: Get there before eight, so you can get a seat.
Keep your ticket safe, because you need it for the bus home.
Check the last bus time before you leave the car park.
Take a coat. The bus stop is miles from the entrance!

body.p: Honestly, I'd choose it over driving every time. Let me know if you try it. Can't wait to hear what you think!
Maya

missions.title: Hire a bike
missions.intro: Three texts about a town's bike hire scheme.

texts.title: Fennbridge Bikes: hire a bike for £1

body.p: Pick up a bike at any of our 20 docking stations and return it to any other station. The first 30 minutes cost just £1. Bikes are available every day from 6 am to 10 pm.

body.callout: I cycle to work now and I save £30 a month on bus fares! - Sam, a Fennbridge Bikes user

body.p: Download our free app to find your nearest bike. You can also see how many bikes are waiting at each station.

texts.title: Fennbridge Bikes: six months on

body.p: Fennbridge Bikes began six months ago with 200 bikes and 20 docking stations. This report looks at how the scheme has been used and suggests ways to improve it. The scheme is run by Vale of Fenn Council and is paid for partly by a grant.

body.h: How many people have used it?

body.p: Since the launch, there have been over 14,000 hires. Saturday is the busiest day, and the most popular journey is from the railway station to Market Square. Most users are commuters and students, and hires are highest in the summer, when the weather is dry and the evenings are light. The council leader said, "The scheme has been a huge success."

The first 30 minutes of every hire cost £1, which is cheaper than the bus fare for the same journey. Bike hire also cuts traffic, which helps to keep the air cleaner. Users who cycle to work every day could save up to £30 a month. Running the scheme costs the council about £2,000 a month, which is covered by hire fees and a grant.

Not everything has gone well. The docking station at the railway station is often full in the evening, so cyclists have to ride to another station to return their bikes. Some bikes have also been damaged, and these must be repaired before they can be used again. Staff visit each docking station every day to move bikes from full stations to empty ones. A small number of users' comments say that there are not enough stations in the east of the town.
The council should add a second docking station near the railway station, buy 50 more bikes and open three new stations in the east of the town. These changes are the best way to improve the scheme.

texts.source: Fennbridge Talk forum, thread: "Anyone tried the bikes?"
texts.title: Re: Anyone tried the bikes?

body.p: Hey everyone! I've been using the bikes for about two months now and honestly I love them.

I live near the market and I work at the hospital, so it takes me ten minutes to get there instead of half an hour on the bus. I also like that you can go through the park, where cars aren't allowed. Honestly, I haven't used my bus pass since, and it's saving me loads of money too. The app is brilliant too. It shows you exactly how many bikes are free at each station.

But there are a few problems. Last Friday I got to the station at about 6 pm and the dock was totally full. I had to cycle round for ages to find a free space, and I nearly missed my train! Also, a couple of the bikes I picked up had wonky brakes, which is scary.
My tips:

ul: Check the app before you set off, so you know where there are free spaces.
Test the brakes before you ride away.
Take the bike back within 30 minutes if you can, because it costs more after that.

body.p: Has anyone else had trouble finding a space at the station?

missions.title: New homes in the village
missions.intro: Three texts about a plan to build new homes in a village.

texts.title: Have your say on new homes in Ashby Green

body.p: Ashby Green Parish Council is holding a meeting about plans to build 40 new homes in the village. Everyone is welcome.
There are three ways to have your say:

ol: Come to the meeting at the village hall on Thursday at 7:30 pm.
Write to the Parish Clerk at the village hall.
Fill in the short form on the council website.

body.p: Please tell us what you think before the end of the month.

texts.title: New homes for Ashby Green: the facts

body.p: Ashby Green Parish Council has been asked to approve plans for 40 new homes on a field beside Church Lane. About 1,200 people live in the village today. This leaflet sets out the main facts so that residents can decide what they think.

There are two main reasons for the plan: the village school has empty places, and the village shop is struggling to stay open. The council hopes that new families will help to keep both going. Over the last ten years, the number of children at the school has fallen and two other shops have closed. Councillor Ruth Barnes says, "The new homes will bring the village back to life."

Twenty-four of the homes will be for sale on the open market, with between two and four bedrooms. Sixteen will be affordable homes, which cost less to buy or rent than most houses in the area. These will be offered first to people who already live or work in the village. All of the new homes will have gardens and parking spaces, and they will be built to use less energy than older houses.

Not everyone is in favour. Some residents are worried about extra traffic on the narrow lanes. One resident, Tom Hendry, says, "The lanes simply cannot cope with more traffic." Others do not want to lose the field, which is used by dog walkers and for the summer fair. The developer says it will pay for a new bus shelter and a safer crossing on Church Lane.

The parish council will meet on Thursday to hear residents' views. The plans must then be approved by the district council, which will decide whether to grant planning permission. A decision is expected within six months.

texts.source: Letter to Ashby Green Parish Council
texts.title: Letter about the Church Lane homes

body.p: Dear Councillors,

I am writing to say that I support the plan to build new homes on Church Lane. I am 19 and I have lived in Ashby Green all my life, but I doubt that I will be able to stay here. Even a small flat in the village costs far more than I can afford on my wage from the garden centre.

Several of my friends have already moved to Brayminster, where there are more homes to rent and the bus runs every fifteen minutes. If the village does not build homes for young people, it will soon have no young people left. I know that some neighbours are worried about traffic, and I understand why. However, I believe a few more cars are a small price to pay for a village that stays alive.
I would therefore ask the council to:

ul: make sure the affordable homes go to local people first
keep a footpath through the field so that walkers can still use it
ask the bus company to run buses more often, as more people will need them

body.p: I would be grateful if you would consider my views at Thursday's meeting.
Yours faithfully,
A resident of Ashby Green

missions.title: Moving to the coast
missions.intro: Three texts about living in a seaside town instead of a city.

texts.title: Welcome to Marram Bay

body.p: Marram Bay is a friendly seaside town with a busy harbour and a lively market.
**Population:** about 9,000
**Distance to Northcaster:** 40 miles
**Trains to Northcaster:** every hour
**Schools:** two primary schools and one secondary school
We hope you will visit us soon, and perhaps even stay.
Our long, sandy beach is open all year, and there is a weekly market on Saturdays. Many families live here because homes cost less than in the city, and the countryside is close by.

texts.title: Should you move to the coast?

body.p: Every year, thousands of people leave the cities for life by the sea. Some want cheaper homes, some want fresh air, and some simply want a change. But is the seaside really the dream it seems?

Property prices in small seaside towns are usually lower than in big cities, so your money often goes further. Estate agent Karen Webb says, "You get more for your money by the sea." There is plenty to do, too, with cafés, shops, boat trips and a market in many towns. Life can also feel calmer, and the beach is often only a short walk from home. Many people also say that the air feels cleaner and that their children have more space to play outdoors.

Many seaside towns have far more visitors in summer than in winter, so a lot of the jobs are seasonal. A café or hotel may employ extra staff from May to September, but then lay them off when the weather turns cold. People who work in cities often have to commute by train, which can be expensive. Some small towns have fewer services too, such as hospitals and large shops, and buses to nearby towns can be infrequent, particularly in the evenings.

Before you move, visit the town in the middle of winter, not just on a sunny weekend in August. Check how often the trains run, how far away the nearest hospital is, and whether there are good schools nearby. Talk to people who already live there, because they will give you an honest view.
Living by the sea is a wonderful experience, and nothing beats waking up to the sound of the waves. With careful planning, it could be the best decision you ever make.

texts.title: One year since we left the city

body.p: A year ago, we swapped a tiny flat in Northcaster for a little house in Marram Bay. Everyone said we were mad, but we've never looked back and we have never been happier.

The house cost far less than our flat would have sold for, and we now have a garden! The beach is five minutes away, and I swim most mornings, even in the cold. I'd never have done that in the city. The winters are wild but beautiful, and we have met more neighbours in a year than in five years in Northcaster.

But it hasn't all been easy. I work at a café on the harbour, and in January there were hardly any customers, so I only had two shifts a week. My partner commutes to Northcaster by train, which costs a fortune, and the last train home is far too early.
My advice if you're thinking of moving:

ul: Visit in winter, not just in summer.
Work out the cost of the train before you buy a house.
Be ready to find a second job for the quiet months.

body.p: Would we move back? No way! But we're a lot wiser than we were.
